topic.title: Object-Oriented Programming
topic.summary: Classes, objects and the four pillars, plus the Java rules (overriding, access, constructors, interfaces) that every junior interview checks.
topic.overview:
## What interviewers expect

OOP comes up in almost every junior interview, and banks, fintechs and service companies that run on Java/Spring or .NET ask about it the most. Expect four kinds of questions:

- **Definitions**: *What is polymorphism?*, *Abstraction vs encapsulation?*
- **Java rules**: *Can we override a static method?*, *What is printed when a constructor calls an overridden method?*
- **"What does this print?"** snippets about static binding, constructor order and field hiding.
- **Small design tasks**: *Model a bank account*, *Design a parking lot* (see SOLID & Design Patterns).

## How to give a strong answer

1. **Definition in one sentence**: say it first and say it clearly.
2. **Concrete example**: a few lines of Java you could write on a whiteboard (`BankAccount`, `Shape`, `PaymentGateway`).
3. **Why / trade-off**: what problem it solves, and when it hurts (for example, inheritance gives you fragile base classes).

## Core concepts in this topic

- **Class vs object**, references, `new`, constructors, `this` / `super`, static vs instance.
- **The four pillars**: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism.
- **Relationships**: is-a (inheritance) vs has-a (composition / aggregation), coupling and cohesion.
- **Java specifics**: access modifiers, overloading vs overriding rules, abstract class vs interface (default methods), the diamond problem.

## How to study

For each question, read the 30-second answer, then close the page and **say it out loud**. Run the code samples and predict the output before you look (to run a Java sample, save it as `Main.java`, or under the name of its `public` class, then run `javac *.java` and `java Main`; the shortcut `java Main.java` only works when the class with `main` comes first in the file). Finish with the quiz: it collects the classic traps (static binding of overloads, constructor order, field hiding, shared class attributes in Python).

cheatsheet.title: The four pillars
points: Encapsulation: private state + methods that guard invariants
Abstraction: expose what, hide how (interface / abstract class)
Inheritance: is-a reuse with extends; Java allows one superclass, many interfaces
Polymorphism: overriding (runtime, dynamic dispatch) and overloading (compile time)

cheatsheet.title: Overloading vs overriding
points: Overloading: same name, different params, chosen from declared types at compile time
Overriding: same signature in a subclass, chosen from the object type at runtime
Return type alone cannot overload; overrides may use a covariant return
Cannot override static (hidden), private (not inherited) or final methods
Overrides cannot narrow access or add broader checked exceptions; use @Override

cheatsheet.title: Java access levels
points: private: the class only
package-private (no keyword): the same package only, not foreign subclasses
protected: the package + subclasses anywhere
public: everyone
Top-level classes: public or package-private

cheatsheet.title: Abstract class vs interface
points: Abstract class: state, constructors, any access; extend one
Interface: no instance state; default/static (8+) and private (9+) methods; implement many
Interface for capabilities and dependency types; abstract class for a template method + shared state

cheatsheet.title: Object creation order (Java)
points: Static blocks once per class, parent first
new: defaults → constructor chain up to Object()
Then per class, parent first: field initialisers + instance blocks, then constructor body
Never call overridable methods from a constructor

cheatsheet.title: Relationships
points: Association: uses another object
Aggregation (o--): has-a, the part can live independently (Team o-- Player)
Composition (*--): owns, shared lifetime (House *-- Room)
Inheritance (<|--) and realisation (<|..)
Favour composition for reuse; keep coupling low and cohesion high

patterns.name: Immutable value class
patterns.whenToUse: Money, coordinates, IDs, DTOs shared between threads. Immutability removes a whole class of bugs.

patterns.name: Template method (abstract class)
patterns.whenToUse: Several subclasses share an algorithm skeleton and state, and differ in one or two steps.

patterns.name: Program to an interface + constructor injection
patterns.whenToUse: Any business class that talks to a database, network or clock. It gives low coupling and easy fakes in tests.

questions.title: What are the four pillars of OOP?
hints: Two pillars are about hiding things, one is about reuse, one is about "many forms".
Think of a Shape hierarchy: what is private, what is abstract, what is extended, what is called in a loop?
Encapsulation = private state + guarded methods; Abstraction = interface/abstract class; Inheritance = extends (is-a); Polymorphism = overriding chosen at runtime.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: Lists the four names with textbook one-liners ("polymorphism means many forms") and no example. It sounds memorised, and it falls apart at the first follow-up.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Defines each pillar in one sentence, ties all four to ONE small example (Shape / Circle / Rectangle), names the Java mechanism (private, interface/abstract, extends, overriding + dynamic dispatch) and says why each exists.

solution.summary: Encapsulation hides an object's state behind methods that protect its rules; abstraction exposes only what an object does through interfaces or abstract classes; inheritance lets a class reuse and specialise another (is-a); polymorphism lets one call run different code depending on the runtime type of the object.
keyPoints: One crisp sentence per pillar, then one example that uses all four
Encapsulation protects invariants (private fields + validating methods), not just "getters and setters"
Abstraction = what, not how (interface / abstract class)
Inheritance is is-a reuse; Java allows one superclass and many interfaces
Polymorphism: overriding (runtime, dynamic dispatch) vs overloading (compile time)
solution.explanation:
**OOP** organises a program around **objects**: units that bundle **state** (fields) with **behaviour** (methods). Four ideas make this work.

### 1. Encapsulation: protect the state
Keep fields `private` and let the outside world change them **only through methods that enforce the rules** (invariants).
- Example: `BankAccount.withdraw()` refuses to make the balance negative. Nobody can write `balance = -100` directly.
- Why: bugs can't corrupt the object from outside, and you can change the internal representation without breaking callers.

### 2. Abstraction: expose *what*, hide *how*
Model only what matters to the caller, as an `interface` or `abstract class`.
- Example: `Shape` promises `area()` and `describe()`. The caller doesn't care how a circle computes its area.
- Why: callers stay simple, and the implementations behind the contract can change or multiply.

### 3. Inheritance: reuse through an *is-a* relationship
A subclass (`Circle extends Shape`) gets the parent's fields and methods and can add or override behaviour.
- Java: a class has exactly **one** superclass, but can implement many interfaces.
- Why: shared code is written once (`describe()` lives only in `Shape`). The risk is tight coupling to the parent, so prefer composition when the relationship is not a true *is-a*.

### 4. Polymorphism: one interface, many forms
The same call does different things depending on the object.
- **Runtime polymorphism (overriding)**: `shape.area()` runs `Circle.area()` or `Rectangle.area()` depending on the actual object. This is called *dynamic dispatch*.
- **Compile-time polymorphism (overloading)**: `print(int)` vs `print(String)`, chosen by the compiler.
- Why: you can add a `Triangle` without touching the loop that prints shapes (open for extension).

### How the pillars work together
In the code sample, **abstraction** defines the contract (`Shape`), **encapsulation** protects each shape's data (`private final radius`), **inheritance** shares `describe()`, and **polymorphism** lets one `for` loop handle every shape.

### Interview script
"Encapsulation hides and protects an object's state behind methods. Abstraction exposes only the essential operations through interfaces or abstract classes. Inheritance lets a class reuse and specialise another class through an is-a relationship. Polymorphism lets the same call behave differently depending on the object's runtime type, as with overriding. For example..." Then show the `Shape` example.

**Abstraction**: `Shape` becomes abstract and promises `area()` without saying how. `describe()` is written once against that promise.

followUps.question: Which pillar do you think matters most in practice?
followUps.answer: A good answer: encapsulation and abstraction (via interfaces) matter most day to day, because they keep code changeable and testable. Inheritance is the one to use most carefully, and composition is often better.

followUps.question: Is OOP possible without classes?
followUps.answer: Yes. JavaScript used prototypes long before the class keyword (which is syntax over prototypes), and Go uses structs + interfaces with no inheritance. The pillars are ideas, not keywords.

questions.title: Class vs object: what happens in memory on new?
hints: One of them exists once per program, the other as many times as you create it.
Where does `new` put the object, and what does the variable actually hold?
`Car c = a;` copies a reference, not the object. Both names point to the same heap object.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "A class is a blueprint and an object is an instance." Correct, but stops there: no memory model and no references.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Blueprint vs instance, plus the mechanics: class loaded once (metadata), `new` allocates on the heap and runs the constructor, the variable holds a reference, `c = a` aliases, `==` compares references, and unreachable objects are garbage-collected.

solution.summary: A class is the blueprint (it declares fields and methods); an object is one instance of it, created with `new` on the heap with its own field values. Variables don't hold objects, they hold references to them, so assigning one variable to another makes both point to the same object.

code.code:
class Car:
    wheels = 4                     # class attribute: shared by all Car objects

    def __init__(self, color):
        self.color = color         # instance attribute: one per object


a = Car("Red")
b = Car("Blue")
c = a                              # same object, two names

c.color = "Green"
print(a.color, b.color)            # Green Blue
print(a is c, a is b)              # True False
print(type(a).__name__, Car.wheels, a.wheels)   # Car 4 4

keyPoints: Class = type/blueprint, loaded once; object = instance with its own state
`new` allocates on the heap, sets defaults, runs the constructor and returns a reference
Assignment copies the reference (aliasing), not the object
`==` compares references; `equals()` compares logical value (override it with hashCode)
Objects with no references left become eligible for garbage collection
solution.explanation:
**A class is a blueprint, and an object is a concrete instance built from it.** A class declares which fields and methods its objects will have. Each object holds its own values for those fields.

| | Class | Object |
|---|---|---|
| What | Type definition / template | Instance with real state |
| How many | One (loaded once by the class loader) | As many as you create |
| Memory (JVM) | Class metadata in **Metaspace** | Fields on the **heap** |
| Created by | Writing code, then the JVM loads it | `new`, reflection, `clone()`, deserialization |

### What `Car a = new Car("Red")` does
1. **Class loading** (first use only): the JVM loads `Car` and runs its static initialisers.
2. **Allocation**: `new` reserves heap memory for one `Car` and sets every field to its default (`null`, `0`, `false`).
3. **Construction**: the constructor runs (`this.color = "Red"`).
4. **Reference**: the local variable `a` (stored in the **stack** frame of `main`) gets a **reference** to that heap object, not the object itself.

### Reference semantics: the classic trap
`Car c = a;` **does not copy the object**. It copies the reference, so `a` and `c` point to the same heap object. Changing `c.color` is visible through `a`.
- `a == c` compares **references**, so it is `true`.
- `a == b` is `false` even if both objects had the same colour. Use `equals()` for logical equality, and override it (plus `hashCode()`) in your class if you need value comparison.

### Garbage collection
When **no reference** points to an object any more (`a = null; c = null;`), it becomes **unreachable** and the garbage collector may reclaim it. You never `free` objects manually in Java, Python or JavaScript.

### Same idea in other languages
Python and JavaScript variables also hold references to objects (`a is c` in Python). In C++ you can also create objects directly on the stack (`Car a("Red");`), which is one reason C++ has copy constructors.

visuals.title: Stack references vs heap objects
visuals.caption: The class is loaded once. Each `new` adds a heap object, and variables only hold references (→ #id) to those objects.

steps.note: The JVM loads class `Car` once. It is only a **blueprint** (one field, one constructor). No `Car` objects exist yet.
`Car a = new Car("Red")`: `new` allocates object **#1** on the heap and runs the constructor. The local variable `a` stores a **reference** to it.
`Car b = new Car("Blue")`: a second, independent object **#2** with its own `color`.
`Car c = a`: **no `new`, so no new object**. `c` gets a copy of the reference, and now `a` and `c` both point to #1.
`c.color = "Green"` follows the reference to object #1 and changes **that object**.
`a.color` prints **Green**, because `a` points to the same object that was changed through `c`. `b.color` is still Blue.
`==` compares **references**: `a == c` is true (same object), `a == b` is false (different objects).
`a = null` removes one reference. Object #1 is still **reachable** through `c`, so it stays alive.
`c = null`: nothing references #1 any more. It is **unreachable**, so the garbage collector may reclaim it. #2 survives because `b` still points to it.

rows: A type: blueprint of fields + methods
An instance of that type with real values
Class metadata in Metaspace; static field values live with its Class object on the heap (HotSpot)
Writing code; the JVM loads it on first use

pitfalls: Thinking `Car c = a;` copies the object: it copies the reference, so changes through c are visible through a
Comparing objects with == when you mean logical equality (e.g. two Strings or two Money objects)
Saying objects live "in the variable". Variables on the stack hold references; objects live on the heap

followUps.question: How do you copy an object then?
followUps.answer: Use a copy constructor or a static factory (`new Car(other)`), or make the class immutable so sharing is safe. `clone()` exists but is error-prone (shallow copy, checked exception). For collections, `new ArrayList<>(list)` or `List.copyOf(list)`.

followUps.question: Is Java pass-by-reference?
followUps.answer: No. Java is always pass-by-value, but for objects the value passed is the reference. A method can mutate the object you passed, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller's variable.

questions.title: What is encapsulation? Why not make fields public?
hints: What could go wrong if any code anywhere could write to `balance`?
Think about a rule the object must always satisfy, and where that rule should be checked.
private fields + methods that validate (deposit/withdraw) + no leaking of mutable internals (return an unmodifiable view).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Encapsulation is making fields private and adding getters and setters." That misses the point: a public setter lets anyone set an invalid value.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Encapsulation keeps state private so that every change goes through methods that enforce invariants. Example: withdraw() rejects overdrafts. Also covers not leaking mutable internals and the freedom to change the representation later.

solution.summary: Encapsulation is bundling data with the methods that operate on it and hiding the data, so every change goes through code that enforces the object's rules. A BankAccount keeps balance private and withdraw() refuses overdrafts, so no caller can ever make the balance negative.
keyPoints: private fields + public behaviour (deposit/withdraw), not public data
Methods enforce invariants (balance never negative)
Do not leak mutable internals: return unmodifiable views or copies
Lets you change the internal representation without breaking callers
Getters/setters for every field is NOT real encapsulation ("tell, don't ask")
solution.explanation:
**Encapsulation means bundling data with the methods that operate on it, and restricting direct access to that data so that every change goes through code that enforces the object's rules.**

### The mechanism
1. Make fields **`private`**.
2. Expose **behaviour**, not raw data: `deposit()`, `withdraw()` instead of `setBalance()`.
3. **Validate** inside those methods so that the invariant (`balance >= 0`) can never be broken.
4. Don't leak mutable internals: return a read-only view or a copy of internal collections (`Collections.unmodifiableList`, `List.copyOf`).

### Why not public fields?
- **Invariants**: with `public long balance`, any line in a 200k-line codebase can write `acc.balance = -100`. With encapsulation, the only door is `withdraw()`, and it says no.
- **Freedom to change internals**: you can switch `long` to `BigDecimal`, add caching or logging, or add thread-safety (`synchronized`) without touching callers.
- **Debugging**: one place to put a breakpoint or audit log for every balance change.
- **Controlled exposure**: secrets such as API keys and PINs are never handed out through the public API. (Access modifiers are a design tool, not a security boundary: reflection can still read private fields.)

### Encapsulation is not "getters and setters for everything"
A class with a public getter and setter for every field is barely better than public fields, because the rules still live outside the class. Prefer **"tell, don't ask"**: `account.withdraw(500)` instead of `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 500)`.

### In other languages
- **Python**: no enforced privacy. `_balance` means "internal" by convention and `__balance` triggers name mangling (`_BankAccount__balance`). A `@property` without a setter makes an attribute read-only.
- **TypeScript**: `private` is checked only at compile time. `#balance` (an ES2022 private field) is enforced at runtime.

### Interview script
"Encapsulation is keeping an object's state private and exposing only methods that maintain its invariants. For example, a `BankAccount` keeps `balance` private, and `withdraw()` rejects amounts larger than the balance, so the balance can never become negative no matter who calls it. It also lets me change the internals later without breaking callers."

visuals.title: Every change goes through the guarded doors
visuals.caption: The only way to change `balance` is through `deposit()` and `withdraw()`, which enforce `balance >= 0`.

steps.note: `new BankAccount("ACC-1001")` starts with balance 0 and an empty history. All three fields are **private**.
`deposit(5000)`: the guard `amount <= 0` is false, so the balance becomes 5000 and the operation is recorded.
`withdraw(8000)`: the guard `amount > balance` (8000 > 5000) **throws** `IllegalStateException`. The state is untouched, so the invariant holds.
`withdraw(1500)` passes both guards, so the balance becomes 3500.
`getBalance()` gives **read** access. There is no `setBalance()`, so reading is allowed and arbitrary writing is not.
`acc.balance = -100` **does not compile** (balance has private access). Outside code cannot go around the rules.
`getHistory().add(...)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, because the getter returns an **unmodifiable view**. Leaking the real list would have been a back door.
Final state: balance 3500 and a history that matches it exactly. **No sequence of calls can break the invariant**, which is what encapsulation buys you.

visuals.title: Public fields vs an encapsulated class

pitfalls: Generating a public setter for every private field: the invariant is then enforced nowhere
Returning the internal mutable List/array/Date from a getter, so callers can modify it behind your back
Assuming Python's __name or TypeScript's private is real security. They are conventions/compile-time checks only (#private is enforced in JS)

followUps.question: How do you make a class fully immutable?
followUps.answer: Make the class final, all fields private final, set them in the constructor, provide no setters, and defensively copy mutable inputs and outputs (or use a Java record with immutable components).

followUps.question: Should money be a double?
followUps.answer: No. Floating point can't represent 0.1 exactly. Use long minor units (paisa/cents) or BigDecimal, and encapsulate it in a Money type.

questions.prompt:
"What is **encapsulation**? Why not just make all fields `public`?"

Show it with a class that has a real **invariant** (a rule that must always hold), for example a bank account whose balance can never go negative.

questions.title: Abstraction vs encapsulation: what is the difference?
hints: Both hide something. Ask what each one hides, and from whom.
One is decided when you design the public contract; the other is enforced inside the class.
Abstraction = what (interface PaymentGateway.pay); encapsulation = how and the data (private apiKey, private helper methods).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Abstraction hides implementation and encapsulation hides data." This is nearly the same sentence twice and doesn't show you understand the difference.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Abstraction is a design-level choice of WHAT to expose (interfaces, abstract classes) to reduce complexity for callers. Encapsulation is an implementation-level technique that protects HOW and the data (private state, validation) to prevent misuse. One example shows both, and you can explain that one can exist without the other.

solution.summary: Abstraction decides what a caller can do and hides the complexity behind a simple contract, such as a PaymentGateway interface with pay(). Encapsulation protects how it is done and the data involved, such as private apiKey and session state inside the implementation. Abstraction reduces complexity for the user; encapsulation prevents misuse.
keyPoints: Abstraction = WHAT (design level, interface / abstract class)
Encapsulation = HOW + data protection (implementation level, private members)
Abstraction reduces complexity for callers; encapsulation protects invariants and secrets
They work together: abstraction draws the boundary, encapsulation enforces it
Concrete example: PaymentGateway.pay() vs private apiKey/sessionToken
solution.explanation:
Both involve hiding, but they hide **different things for different reasons**.

### Abstraction: hide complexity, show *what*
Abstraction is a **design** decision. It decides **which operations a caller needs** and hides everything else behind a simple contract.
- Tools: `interface`, `abstract class`, a well-chosen public method name.
- Example: `PaymentGateway.pay(phone, amount)`. `CheckoutService` neither knows nor cares whether money moves through a mobile wallet, a card network or a test fake.
- Benefit: implementations can be swapped or multiplied without touching callers.

### Encapsulation: hide and protect data, enforce *how*
Encapsulation is an **implementation** technique. It keeps an object's **state and internal steps** private, so they can only be reached through controlled methods.
- Tools: `private` fields, private helper methods, validation inside public methods, immutable fields.
- Example: inside `MobileWalletGateway`, `apiKey`, `sessionToken`, `requestCount` and `ensureSession()` are all private. Nobody outside can read the key or skip the session step.
- Benefit: invariants hold and secrets don't leak.

### One sentence each
- **Abstraction** = *"what does it do?"*. It reduces **complexity** for the user of a class.
- **Encapsulation** = *"how is it protected?"*. It reduces **damage**: no outside code can break the object.

### How they work together
Abstraction draws the **boundary** (the public contract). Encapsulation **enforces** it (everything else is private). You can have one without the other:
- A class with all-public fields but a clean interface has abstraction without encapsulation.
- A class with private fields but 40 confusing public methods that leak implementation details has encapsulation without much abstraction.

### Analogy
A car's steering wheel and pedals are the **abstraction**: any driver can drive any car. The sealed engine bay and the ECU that rejects unsafe RPM are the **encapsulation**.

followUps.question: Can you have encapsulation without abstraction?
followUps.answer: Yes. A class can keep all fields private yet expose a confusing API that leaks implementation details (e.g. `setInternalRetryBufferSize`). The data is protected, but callers still face all the complexity.

followUps.question: Where do you see abstraction in Spring?
followUps.answer: `JpaRepository`, `RestClient`, `PlatformTransactionManager`: you code against interfaces and Spring supplies the implementation (Hibernate, a JDBC transaction manager, etc.).

questions.title: Types of inheritance and the diamond problem
hints: List the shapes a hierarchy can take: one parent, a chain, a fan-out, two parents.
With two parents that share a grandparent, which version of a method does the child get, and how many copies of the grandparent exist?
Java: one superclass only; interface default conflicts must be overridden (X.super.m()); class wins. Python: C3 MRO + super(). C++: virtual inheritance.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Java doesn't support multiple inheritance because of the diamond problem." Incomplete: it ignores interfaces and default methods, and doesn't explain the problem itself.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Names all five types, explains the two halves of the diamond problem (ambiguous method + duplicated base state), and shows how Java (single class inheritance, default-method resolution rules), C++ (virtual inheritance) and Python (C3 MRO) solve it.

solution.summary: Inheritance can be single, multilevel, hierarchical, multiple or hybrid. Java classes allow only single inheritance (one superclass), but a class can implement many interfaces. The diamond problem (two parents sharing a grandparent) appears with Java 8 default methods, and Java resolves it by making the class override the conflicting method and pick a parent with Interface.super.method().
keyPoints: Five types: single, multilevel, hierarchical, multiple, hybrid
Java: one superclass, many interfaces, so no state diamond
Default-method conflicts: class wins > more specific interface wins > else compile error, resolve with X.super.m()
C++ uses virtual inheritance to share the base; Python uses the C3 MRO and cooperative super()
Use inheritance only for true is-a relationships; prefer composition for reuse
solution.explanation:
**Inheritance** lets a class (the subclass) acquire the fields and methods of another class (the superclass) and add or override behaviour. It models an **is-a** relationship: `SavingsAccount` *is an* `Account`.

### Types of inheritance
| Type | Shape | Java classes? |
|---|---|---|
| **Single** | `B extends A` | Yes |
| **Multilevel** | `C extends B extends A` | Yes |
| **Hierarchical** | `B`, `C`, `D` all extend `A` | Yes |
| **Multiple** | `C` extends both `A` and `B` | **No** for classes, **yes** for interfaces |
| **Hybrid** | a mix, often containing a diamond | Only through interfaces |

### The diamond problem
`Camera` and `Phone` both inherit from `Device` and both override `start()`. If `SmartPhone` inherits from **both**, then:
1. Which `start()` does `SmartPhone` get?
2. Does `SmartPhone` contain **one** `Device` part or **two**?

### Java's answer
- **Classes**: a class can extend only **one** class, so the state part of the diamond cannot happen.
- **Interfaces**: a class can implement many. Before Java 8, interfaces had no method bodies, so there was nothing to conflict. Since **Java 8 default methods**, two interfaces can supply bodies with the same signature. The rules are:
  1. **Class wins**: a method inherited from a superclass beats any interface default (`Tablet extends Device implements Camera` gets `Device.start()`).
  2. **More specific interface wins**: if `B extends A` and both define the default, `B`'s version is used.
  3. Otherwise it is a **compile error** ("types Camera and Phone are incompatible"). The class must override the method and may call `Camera.super.start()` and/or `Phone.super.start()` explicitly.
- Interfaces carry **no instance state**, so there is never a "two copies of the base" problem.

### C++
Multiple class inheritance is allowed. Without care, `SmartPhone` contains **two** `Device` sub-objects and an unqualified call is ambiguous. **Virtual inheritance** (`class Camera : virtual public Device`) shares a single `Device`.

### Python
Multiple inheritance is allowed. Python computes a **Method Resolution Order (MRO)** with the **C3 linearisation**: `SmartPhone → Camera → Phone → Device → object`. Each class appears once, children come before parents, and the left parent comes before the right. `super()` means "the next class in the MRO", not "my parent", so `Camera.start()`'s `super()` call reaches `Phone`, and `Device.start()` runs exactly once.

### When not to inherit
Use inheritance only for a true *is-a* that respects the parent's contract (the Liskov Substitution Principle). For reuse, prefer composition.

solution.explanation:
**Polymorphism** ("many forms") means one name or one call can behave differently. Java has two kinds, and they are decided at **different times**.

### Overloading: compile-time (static) polymorphism
- Same method name, **different parameter lists** (number, type or order), usually in the same class.
- The **compiler** picks the overload from the **declared (static) types** of the arguments. The runtime type is ignored.
- `Object o = "hello"; p.print(o)` calls `print(Object)`, because the compiler only knows that `o` is an `Object`.
- The return type alone cannot distinguish overloads (`int f()` and `String f()` is a compile error).
- Overload resolution happens in phases: an exact or widening match first, then boxing/unboxing, then varargs. That's why `print(42)` prefers `print(int)` over `print(Object)`.

### Overriding: runtime (dynamic) polymorphism
- A **subclass** redefines an inherited instance method with the **same signature**.
- The **JVM** picks the implementation from the **actual object type** at runtime (*dynamic dispatch*, implemented with a per-class method table, the "vtable").
- `Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound()` prints `Woof`.
- Rules: same parameters; the return type may be the same or a subtype (*covariant*); access cannot be **narrowed** (`public` → `protected` is an error); you cannot throw new or broader **checked** exceptions; use `@Override` so the compiler catches typos.

### What cannot be overridden
- **static** methods are **hidden**, not overridden. `a.kind()` calls `Animal.kind()` because static calls bind to the declared type.
- **private** methods are not inherited, so a same-named method in a subclass is a brand-new method.
- **final** methods cannot be overridden. Constructors are never inherited.
- **Fields** are not polymorphic either: `P obj = new C(); obj.name` reads `P`'s field (field hiding).

### Why it matters
Overriding is what makes the Open/Closed principle work: code written against `Animal` or `PaymentGateway` automatically uses new subclasses. Overloading is mostly a convenience for callers (`Math.max(int, int)` / `Math.max(double, double)`).

### Other languages
- **Python / JavaScript**: overriding works the same way. There is **no signature-based overloading**: a second `def` with the same name replaces the first. Use default arguments, `*args`, or `functools.singledispatch`, which dispatches on the runtime type of the first argument.
- **TypeScript**: overload *signatures* exist for type-checking, but there is only one implementation body.

solution.explanation:
### Short version
- An **interface** is a **contract or capability**: *"anything that is `Refundable` can `refund()`"*. Unrelated classes can implement it, and a class can implement many.
- An **abstract class** is a **partially built base class**: shared **state**, **constructors** and **code** for a family of closely related classes. A class can extend only one.

### What changed in Java 8 and 9
- **Java 8**: interfaces gained **`default` methods** (bodies that implementers inherit) and **`static` methods**. The main motivation was **evolving APIs**: `Collection.stream()` and `Iterable.forEach()` were added as defaults, so millions of existing implementations kept compiling.
- **Java 9**: **`private` interface methods**, to share code between defaults.
- Interfaces **still cannot** have instance fields (only `public static final` constants) or constructors. That is the real remaining difference: **an interface has no state**.

### Detailed differences
| | Abstract class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple inheritance | Extend one | Implement many |
| Instance fields | Yes | No (constants only) |
| Constructors | Yes | No |
| Method access | Any (`private`, `protected`, ...) | Implicitly `public`, plus `private` helpers (Java 9+) |
| Concrete methods | Yes | `default` / `static` (Java 8+) |
| Typical role | Template method, shared base code | Capability, API boundary, dependency for injection |

### When to use which
- **Interface** (the default choice): defining what a dependency can do (`PaymentGateway`, `UserRepository`), capabilities that cut across hierarchies (`Comparable`, `AutoCloseable`), lambdas (functional interfaces such as `Runnable`).
- **Abstract class**: several closely related classes share **state and an algorithm skeleton**. Example: `Payment.process()` is a `final` **template method** that counts attempts and validates, and leaves only `charge()` to subclasses.
- A common combination: an interface as the public type, plus an abstract base class that implements it for convenience (`List` + `AbstractList`).

### Modern Java notes
- **Sealed** interfaces and classes (Java 17) restrict who may implement or extend them, which is useful for closed hierarchies (`sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square`).
- **Records** can implement interfaces but cannot extend classes.

The **template method** `process()` is final and fixes the algorithm. Subclasses only fill in the `charge()` step. An interface cannot do this because it has no `attempts` field to update.

questions.title: Composition vs inheritance: why "favour composition"?

Classic example: a HashSet subclass that counts adds. addAll() internally calls add(), so every element is counted twice. Wrapping (delegation) fixes it.

approaches.name: Weak answer

approaches.name: Strong answer

solution.summary: Inheritance couples a subclass to its parent's implementation, so a change or a hidden self-call in the parent can break it (the fragile base class problem). Composition holds another object and delegates to its public interface, which is looser, can be swapped at runtime and is easier to test. Default to composition; use inheritance for true is-a relationships with classes designed for extension.
keyPoints: Inheritance = is-a, fixed at compile time; composition = has-a, swappable at runtime
Fragile base class: the subclass depends on the parent's internal self-calls (addAll → add)

Use inheritance for real subtypes (LSP) and classes designed for extension
solution.explanation:
- **Inheritance** (*is-a*): `class CountingHashSet extends HashSet`. You reuse code by becoming a subtype.
- **Composition** (*has-a*): `class CountingSet { private final Set inner; }`. You reuse code by holding another object and **delegating** to it.

### The classic bug: the fragile base class
We want a set that counts how many elements were ever added (example adapted from *Effective Java*).
1. `CountingHashSet` overrides `add()` (`addCount++`) and `addAll()` (`addCount += c.size()`).
2. `addAll(["a","b","c"])` adds 3, then calls `super.addAll(c)`.
3. `HashSet` inherits `addAll` from `AbstractCollection`, which **calls `add()` for each element**, and because of dynamic dispatch that is **our** overridden `add()`.
4. Each element is counted twice: **`addCount == 6`**.

Our class broke because it depended on an **internal implementation detail** of its parent. That detail isn't part of `HashSet`'s contract, so a future JDK could change it either way. With **composition**, `CountingSet` only forwards to `inner.addAll()`. The inner set calls *its own* `add()`, never ours, so the count is a correct **3**.

### Why composition is the usual default
- **Loose coupling**: you depend only on the public interface of the part.
- **Runtime flexibility**: swap the part (`employee.policy = new ManagerPolicy()` on promotion). An object can never change its class.
- **Selective exposure**: forward only the methods you want. A `Stack extends Vector` (a real JDK mistake) exposes `insertElementAt()`, which breaks the stack's rules.
- **Testability**: inject a fake part.
- Composition powers patterns such as **Strategy**, **Decorator**, **Adapter** and **dependency injection**.

### When inheritance is right
- A genuine subtype relationship that passes **Liskov substitution**: every `Circle` can be used wherever a `Shape` is expected.
- The parent is **designed and documented for extension** (abstract classes with template methods, framework base classes).
- Otherwise make classes `final` or keep the hierarchy shallow.

### Interview script
"Inheritance couples the subclass to the parent's implementation. In the counting-set example, overriding `add` and `addAll` double-counts because `HashSet.addAll` internally calls `add`. Composition wraps the set and delegates, so it depends only on the public contract and gives the right answer. I default to composition and use inheritance only for true is-a relationships with classes designed for extension."

steps.note: `s1.addAll(["a","b","c"])` enters **our** override: `addCount += c.size()`, so addCount = 3.
`super.addAll(c)`: `HashSet` does not define `addAll`. It inherits `AbstractCollection.addAll`, which simply loops and calls **`add(e)`** for each element.
`add("a")` is a virtual call on our object, so dynamic dispatch picks **our** `CountingHashSet.add`, and addCount++ makes it **4**.
`add("b")`: counted again, so addCount = **5**.
`add("c")`: addCount = **6**.
The set holds 3 elements but addCount is **6**. Our class broke because it relied on a **hidden implementation detail** of its parent: the fragile base class problem.
Composition: `s2.addAll(...)` adds 3, then forwards to `inner.addAll(c)`. The inner HashSet calls **its own** `add`, because our `CountingSet.add` is not part of its object.
Result: **addCount = 3**, correct, and it stays correct whatever `HashSet` does internally, because we depend only on the public `Set` contract.

frames.note: **Inheritance**: `CountingHashSet` *is a* `HashSet`. It inherits every public method, including ones that break its counting rule.
**Composition**: `CountingSet` *has a* `Set` and forwards to it. Any `Set` implementation can be wrapped.

So construction climbs to Object first; then each class, parent first, runs its field initialisers and instance blocks, then its constructor body. solution.explanation:
A **constructor** initialises a new object. It has the class's name, no return type, and is **not inherited**. If you write none, the compiler adds a no-argument **default constructor** that just calls `super()`.

### `this` and `super`
- `this.x`: the current object's field (useful when a parameter has the same name).
- `this(args)`: call **another constructor of the same class**. This is constructor chaining, and it avoids duplicated initialisation code.
- `super.method()`: call the parent's version of an overridden method.
- `super(args)`: call a **parent constructor**. If you don't write `this(...)` or `super(...)`, the compiler inserts `super()`. If the parent has no no-arg constructor, that is a **compile error**.
- In Java 21, `this(...)` / `super(...)` must be the **first statement**, so a constructor can use only one of them. (Java 25's *flexible constructor bodies* allow statements before them, as long as they don't use `this`.)

### Order of execution for `new Child()`
1. **Class initialisation, once per class, parent first**: `Base` static blocks, then `Child` static blocks.
2. Memory is allocated, and every field gets its default value (`null`, `0`, `false`).
3. `Child()` starts and immediately calls `super()`, which climbs the chain (`Base()` → `this("default")` → `Base(String)` → `Object()`).
4. After `Object()` returns, **`Base`'s field initialisers and instance blocks** run (in textual order), then the rest of the `Base(String)` body, then the rest of `Base()`.
5. Back in `Child`: **`Child`'s field initialisers and instance blocks** run, then the `Child()` body.

So the rule is: **parents before children, statics once, and initialisers right after the `super(...)` call returns**.

### The trap: calling an overridable method from a constructor
`Base(String)` calls `hook()`. Because of dynamic dispatch, the **child's** `hook()` runs, but `Child`'s fields are not initialised yet, so it sees `city = null` (or `0` for an `int`). This causes subtle `NullPointerException`s. Rule: **constructors should call only `private`, `static` or `final` methods.**

### Python comparison
Python's `__init__` is an initialiser, not a constructor (`__new__` creates the object). The parent's `__init__` **is not called automatically**: forget `super().__init__()` and the parent's attributes never exist.

solution.summary: Static members belong to the class: there is one copy, shared by all objects, reached through the class name. Instance members belong to each object, which gets its own copy. A static method has no `this`, so it cannot touch instance fields directly, and static methods are bound at compile time (hidden, not overridden).

solution.explanation:
- **Instance members** belong to **each object**. Every `User` has its own `id` and `name`.
- **Static members** belong to the **class itself**. There is exactly **one** `totalUsers` no matter how many `User` objects exist (strictly, one per class per class loader).

### Mechanism
- Static fields are created when the class is **initialised** and live until the class is unloaded. They are reached as `User.totalUsers`.
- Instance fields are created by `new`, stored inside each heap object, and reached through a reference (`a.name`).
- A **static method has no `this`**: it is called on the class, so there is no "current object". Writing `return name;` inside `getTotalUsers()` doesn't compile, because the compiler can't know *whose* name you mean. Pass an object in if you need one.
- An instance method can use both instance and static members.

### Static and polymorphism
Static methods are **bound at compile time** to the declared type. A subclass method with the same signature **hides** the parent's static method instead of overriding it, so `Animal a = new Dog(); a.kind()` calls `Animal.kind()`.

### Good uses of `static`
- **Constants**: `static final double TAX_RATE = 0.15;`
- **Factory / utility methods** that don't need object state: `List.of()`, `Math.max()`, `Integer.parseInt()`, `User.fromJson(...)`.
- **Shared counters / caches**, used with care.
- **Static nested classes**, such as a `Builder` that doesn't need a reference to an outer instance.

### Dangers
- **Mutable static state is global state**: every thread and every test shares it. `totalUsers++` is not thread-safe (use `AtomicInteger`), and tests leak state into each other.
- Overusing static methods makes code hard to mock and pushes you towards procedural design.

### Python note
Class attributes are shared, but **assigning through an instance creates an instance attribute** that shadows the class attribute (`a.count += 1`). A mutable class attribute such as `items = []` is shared by all instances, which is a frequent bug.

solution.explanation:
Java has **four** access levels, from most to least restrictive:

| Modifier | Same class | Same package | Subclass in another package | Everywhere else |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `private` | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| *(none)*: package-private | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ |
| `protected` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ (through inheritance) | ✗ |
| `public` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

### Two facts that surprise people
1. **`protected` includes package access.** `Teller`, which is in the same package as `Account` but is *not* a subclass, can read `a.balance`.
2. **Package-private excludes subclasses in other packages.** `SavingsAccount` in `com.bank.app` cannot see `branchCode`, even though it extends `Account`.

### The fine print of `protected`
A subclass in another package can access a protected member only **through references of its own type (or subtypes)**: `this.balance` or `otherSavings.balance` work, but `new Account().balance` inside `SavingsAccount` is a compile error. The access exists so that a subclass can manage **its own inherited part**, not so it can poke into arbitrary `Account` objects.

### Other rules
- **Top-level classes** can only be `public` or package-private (one public top-level class per `.java` file, matching the file name).
- When **overriding**, you may widen access (`protected` → `public`) but never narrow it.
- Interface members are implicitly `public` (except Java 9+ `private` helpers).
- Reflection (`setAccessible(true)`) can bypass access checks unless the module system blocks it, so **access modifiers are a design tool, not a security boundary**.
- Since Java 9, **modules** (`module-info.java`) add another layer: a `public` class is visible outside its module only if its package is `exports`-ed.

### Rule of thumb
Start with **`private`** and widen only when needed: fields `private`, helpers `private`, the public API `public`, and extension points for subclasses `protected`. Package-private is useful for classes that are internal to a feature package and for tests in the same package.

**protected** (`balance`): the same package (yes, `Teller` too) **plus** subclasses anywhere, through inheritance (`this.balance`, or another `SavingsAccount`). `Main` in another package is denied.
**public** (`owner`): visible everywhere the class itself is visible.

The full picture. The two cells people get wrong: **protected includes the package** and **package-private excludes foreign subclasses**. Rule of thumb: start `private`, widen only when a caller really needs it.

hints: One is about relationships between classes; the other is about what is inside one class.

solution.summary: Coupling is how much one module depends on others; cohesion is how closely the responsibilities inside one module belong together. Aim for low coupling and high cohesion, so a change stays local, classes are easy to understand and test, and parts can be swapped. In practice: one responsibility per class, and depend on injected interfaces instead of concrete classes.
keyPoints: Coupling = between modules (want LOW); cohesion = within a module (want HIGH)
Tight coupling smell: `new ConcreteThing()` inside business logic, long getter chains, shared globals

Raise cohesion: Single Responsibility Principle; split "Manager/Utils" god classes
Payoff: local changes, easy testing with fakes, parallel work by different developers
solution.explanation:
- **Coupling** is how strongly one module (class, package, service) **depends on another**. Low coupling means a change in one rarely forces a change in the other.
- **Cohesion** is how strongly the responsibilities **inside one module belong together**. High cohesion means a class does one focused job.

They are two sides of good modular design: **high cohesion inside, low coupling between**.

### Before: low cohesion and tight coupling
`OrderManager.placeOrder()` validates the order, opens a `new MySqlConnection(...)`, sends mail with `new SmtpMailer(...)`, builds a PDF invoice and updates loyalty points.
- **Low cohesion**: five unrelated reasons to change the class.
- **Tight coupling**: it creates concrete classes itself, so you can't test it without a database and a mail server, and switching email to SMS means editing order logic.

### After: high cohesion and loose coupling
- `OrderService` only places orders. `InvoiceService` builds PDFs. `LoyaltyService` handles points.
- `OrderService` depends on small **interfaces** (`OrderRepository`, `Notifier`) that are **injected through the constructor** (dependency injection).
- Production wires `MySqlOrderRepository` + `SmsNotifier`. Tests wire `InMemoryOrderRepository` + `ConsoleNotifier`. Adding `EmailNotifier` means adding a class and changing the wiring, while `OrderService` stays untouched.

### Ways to lower coupling
- Depend on **interfaces**, not concrete classes (Dependency Inversion).
- **Inject** dependencies instead of calling `new` inside business logic.
- **Encapsulate**: hide fields so others can't depend on internals.
- Communicate through **events or messages** (Observer, message queues) when the sender doesn't need to know the receivers.
- Apply the *Law of Demeter* ("talk to friends, not strangers"): avoid `order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity()` chains.

### Ways to raise cohesion
- **Single Responsibility Principle**: one reason to change.
- Move a method to the class whose data it uses most.
- Be suspicious of names like `Manager`, `Helper` or `Utils`, and of names that need "and".

### Textbook scales (asked in some university-style interviews)
- **Coupling**, worst to best: content → common (global data) → external → control (passing flags) → stamp (passing whole structures) → data (passing only the needed values).
- **Cohesion**, worst to best: coincidental → logical → temporal → procedural → communicational → sequential → functional.

Interface methods can never have a body
